Sciviz `/flow` supplies fixed-step RK4 pathlines/streaklines and GPU particles/trails on regular 2D/3D grids
with linear temporal interpolation. Adaptive error control and extrapolation are not supplied. The default
10,000-step budget accepts 1 to 1,000,000; at most 4,096 frames. CPU input copies plus
output/final-copy/scratch are capped at 128 MiB, excluding caller input and module overhead. Copy/integration
chunks are 16,384 samples/128 steps. The feature-local Wasm is 7,916 bytes, capped below 16,000 raw and 8,000 gzip
by CPU tests. It loads lazily per call; root/fallback do not load it. Samples are float32 and arithmetic/output
float64. Streaklines reuse one instance/field copy for 1..4096 ordered releases, returning observation-time
endpoints and NaN gaps for invalid/unfinished releases. GPU transport is forward only; each RK stage uses
float32 normalised coordinates/velocities, with four stages and an accepted-endpoint validity check. The
analytic GPU/CPU test bound is 0.0002 distance units on its stated fields, not a general error guarantee.
GPU layer creation copies fields; its 1..1000000 particles and 2..256 history samples (defaults 1024/32)
must fit 128 MiB of GPU buffers and device binding/buffer limits. CPU copies are additional. Bounds/widths
must survive float32; normalised velocities and step-times-velocity are at most float32 max/16 for arithmetic
headroom. Lifetime defaults to 10 time units, expires at step endpoints and fixed-seed respawn defaults true.
Width defaults 2 device pixels (positive, at most 64), opacity 0.8, sRGB colour #7ddcff. Heads are squares;
history fades quadratically and never bridges respawn generations. Uniform/random/rake/region seed layouts
are deterministic for a given seed/partition on one backend; cross-device bit identity is unclaimed.
Actual device replacement replays accepted partitions, bounded by maxSteps; advance/draw do no position
readback. Explicit readPositions has a 30000 ms default timeout. WebGPU and WebGL2 compatibility pass
numeric/pixel/lifecycle tests; native WebGL2 flow remains pending with batch 181. NOAA daily means do not
establish observed tracks or forecast accuracy. The official Moving wind example preserves these limitations.
The `/flow` JavaScript entry is 8,665 B gzip (raised optional ceiling 8,854 B);
the previous CPU-only size was 2,130 B (ceiling 2,386 B). Root remains 36,916 B, driver 4,476 B, Wasm 7,916 raw /
3,585 gzip B; their ceilings are unchanged by flow. Keeping one coherent flow entry avoids an artificial loader
between transport, seed semantics and owned replay state.
No core/stage implementation change is part of this feature.

`npm run test:speed` does no measurement while deferred. After Scott ends the
build phase, `MARGO_SPEED_PHASE=active` runs the named suite on a quiet machine,
sequentially with bounded commands. Its entire inventory must pass before release,
along with an empty busy-retest list. Deferral makes no speed or GPU-quality claim. Every build-phase exclusive request
is refused and logged unless the coordinator records Scott's approval for that

New GPU clients retain FIFO admission tickets for shared and exclusive requests.
Detached `gpu-lock.mjs enqueue` submissions retain the 60-minute default gate
wait; `wait <ticket>` observes the same request and never cancels it on timeout.
Status records persist beside the lock, and command logs stay in the submitting
worktree. Older clients remain interoperable but keep their older ordering;
Eligible-lane FIFO applies only to new clients. A shared eligible head request needs one free slot,
not an empty GPU. Commands and observers each have a hard time limit.

Exclusive GPU holds are reserved for classified speed commands or an explicit,
logged timing reason, with a 20-minute maximum including wrapper overhead.
Oversize holds and correctness requests fail before waiting and are recorded in
`test-results/gpu-lock-refusals.log`. Long matrices must release between bounded
suites. This scheduling cap is based on existing 88.4/113.3/184.4-second benchmark
records, not a new measurement on the busy build machine.

GPU scheduling mutexes publish owner identity atomically and reclaim only an
identified dead process. A live or anonymous legacy mutex is never reclaimed by
age; its owner's release is required. Acquisition has a bounded wait (default
60 minutes, `--wait-max` / `MARGO_GPU_WAIT_MAX_MIN`), including mutex contention.
An independent one-second refresh preserves the old reader/writer client's
ten-second freshness convention during synchronous work. Holder/waiter formats
remain compatible. This is CPU-only scheduling evidence, not a GPU speed claim.

Native WebGL2 live rebuild and disposal release the preview renderer's current program before deleting it.
A foreign current program is preserved. The lifetime regression covers both operations and catches a deleted
binding escaping into another plugin's state scope; it adds no rendering feature or timing claim.

Half-float voxel encoding uses one reusable four-byte bit-cast buffer, with no typed-array allocations per voxel.
It retains IEEE binary16 rounding, subnormals and special values. This changes neither brick selection nor the
atlas budget; `tests/f16-allocation.test.js` checks all 65,536 half words, rounding ties and allocation counts.

Voxel streaming memory admission (2026-11-09): `VoxelStreamer.memoryBudget` limits loaded chunk typed-array
bytes, not total process memory. Both ready and loading jobs reserve the loaded chunks' mean size; a finished
stored or generated chunk joins only when its actual `byteLength` fits after LRU eviction outside the load range.
A chunk that cannot fit remains pending, including one larger than the entire budget. Initial unknown-size loads,
pending results, workers, stores and failed saves are outside this budget. Edits, externally added chunks and
budget reductions can leave the protected load range over budget; further admission stops. Deterministic stored,
variable-size and packed-worker regressions are in `packages/voxel/tests/streamer.test.js`.

Sciviz restoration (2026-11-10): CPU-backed layers rebuild on a replacement device; `Figure.ready()` waits for
isosurface reconstruction. Pending old-device extractions reject with code `state`. Caller-owned GPU arrays
cannot survive device loss without a CPU copy: their layers hide and must be recreated on the replacement
device. CPU isosurfaces retain 4 bytes per voxel; meshes retain positions, normals and values (28 bytes per
corner), graphs retain 12 bytes per node for positions plus 4 bytes per node value and 8 bytes per edge, and map
tiles retain 4 bytes per decoded pixel for restoration. Bricked volumes reread their source.
3D axis labels use 8 CSS pixels of clearance; crowded tick labels are omitted, with data ticks and grid lines
unchanged. Active bricked frame aborts cancel source signals and late publication; standalone `ready` aborts
cancel only the wait. Regression coverage: `packages/sciviz/tests/restoration-browser.mjs`,
`entries-browser.js`, `updates.test.js` and `demos-browser.mjs` (head/stars at 390 x 844 and 1440 x 900).

Sciviz volume and isosurface grids require integer dimensions of at least two samples per axis; single slices
belong in a 2D `Figure.heatmap`. Axis errors are reported separately from mismatched sample counts.
Overlapping isosurface extractions and bricked frame requests run in request order. An isosurface extraction
holds the displayed and pending vertex buffers (96 bytes per triangle in each); an aborted or failed extraction
keeps the displayed surface. `Figure.replace(old, next)` rebuilds a trace and briefly holds both layers rather
than updating its buffers in place. Await the replacement builder and call `replace` immediately, with no render
or wait between them. Serialize asynchronous changes with `Figure.timeline`; a disposed timeline does not
cancel user callback work. These guarantees are covered by the sciviz unit and browser suites; no speed claim.

Margo is a small WebGPU engine: core plus the stage facade is 24,209 B gzip (`npm run measure:size` prints the exact figure; the build fails at 25,000 bytes; core alone is 21,584 B of its 21,587 B cap (2026-11-09: core uploads the unit light direction so no shader normalizes that uniform-only value, core 21,553 B to 21,584 B and core + stage 23,924 B to 23,950 B; 2026-11-07: `CADCameraControls` moved to the stage, core 21,586 B to 20,672 B and core + stage 23,013 B to 23,016 B; stable instance rows with changed-row uploads then added 382 B and `Engine.writePoses` 231 B, so core + stage was 23,626 B; CSP diagnostics then added 171 B, taking it to 23,837 B); the 2026-10-30 core cleanup, which removed the view target depth copy pass, `mesh.euler` and four small duplicates, took core from 21,176 B to 20,790 B and core + stage from 22,580 B to 22,189 B; storing a caller's 4x view target depth then added 23 B to each, a package's frame in one render pass 293 B to core + stage, and `Engine.renderTarget` 44 B), and every
other capability is an optional package. That size is a decision, and so are the boundaries below. Each one exists
for one of two reasons: it keeps core small and frozen, or it follows the limits WebGPU guarantees on every adapter
(Margo's device requests none above them, so an app that runs on a laptop also runs on a phone). This page lists every
hard limit, where it starts, what you see when you reach it, and the package or tool that takes you past it.

How to read "Starts at":

- **Enforced**: an exact constant in the source (linked), usually with the test that asserts it.
- **Measured**: a committed result file (linked). Unless a row says otherwise: ASUS Zenbook S 14, Intel Core Ultra 7
  258V with an Intel Arc 140V integrated GPU, Windows 11, Edge 155, AC power, GPU lock held.
- **Not measured**: the boundary exists, but nobody has run the case. No number is given.

Every number here has a row in [whitepaper/claims.md](whitepaper/claims.md) (LIM-001 to LIM-656). Past losses and their
fixes are in [whitepaper/perf-history.md](whitepaper/perf-history.md).

## Scale

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entities (core meshes, assembly nodes included) | Enforced: 8,388,608 slots (2^23; [kernel.ts](../packages/core/src/kernel.ts), [core-dirty-transforms.test.js](../tests/core-dirty-transforms.test.js)). The store starts at `capacity` (default 1,024) and doubles on demand. Measured ([results-scale-node.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/parts/results-scale-node.json), Node 24, quiet-gated): 352.1 B of kernel memory per slot at 1,048,576 slots (351 B by layout); a static kernel tick costs 3.3 ms at 100,006 entities, 20.2 ms at 499,992 and 41.5 ms at 1,000,012. Above 1,048,576 slots: not measured. | One float32 structure-of-arrays Wasm kernel computes every transform, bound and visibility. It is the reason core is small and fast, and its per-entity cost is linear: about 41 ns per entity per frame even when nothing moves. | Growth is automatic. Past the cap `createMesh` throws `RangeError: Capacity`; `Engine.create` with a larger `capacity` throws `RangeError: Capacity: 1..8388608`. A growth that cannot allocate throws and leaves the store as it was. Before the cap, frame time grows with entity count. | `@margoengine/culling`. `CulledInstances` keeps parts out of the entity store entirely: 0.41-0.55 ms CPU per frame at 89,883 parts, flat in part count ([results-culling.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/parts/results-culling.json)); parts lose picking, hierarchy and section caps. `CulledMeshes` GPU-culls parts that must stay core meshes; it removes GPU work, not the kernel tick. |
| Nodes and parts per file in packages | Enforced, default 100,000 ([limits.js](../packages/shared/limits.js), [count-limits.test.js](../tests/count-limits.test.js)): glTF nodes ([gltf](../packages/gltf/src/index.ts), [gltf-pro asset.ts](../packages/gltf-pro/src/asset.ts)), `.margo` nodes ([blender](../packages/blender/src/index.ts)). | Input validation that bounds memory for untrusted files: every node or part becomes a core mesh. | `RangeError: Too many glTF nodes (100001 > 100000; raise the maxNodes option)`; likewise `Too many .margo nodes` (`maxNodes`). | The option the error names, up to core's 8,388,608 entities: `maxNodes` on the glTF, gltf-pro and `.margo` loaders; a value outside 1 to 8,388,608 throws `maxNodes must be an integer from 1 to 8388608`. Load time and memory past 100,000: not measured. |
| Buffers per geometry | Enforced: a geometry's vertex, index and instance buffers (96 B per instance) must each fit the device's `maxBufferSize`; core requests the WebGPU default ([renderer.ts](../packages/core/src/renderer.ts)). Not measured. | WebGPU's guaranteed limits, so the same scene runs on every adapter. | `RangeError: GPU buffer limit` when the geometry is first drawn. | Split the geometry, or draw the copies with `CulledInstances`. |
| Instance rows after culling flips (2026-11-07) | By method: a mesh that culling or `visible` shows takes its batch's next row and one hidden gives its row to the batch's last, so row order inside a batch, and with it draw order among one geometry's instances, follows the order of flips. Proved exact as a set, row for row and in the uploaded GPU rows on 200 random frames of flips and moves ([core-instance-cache.test.js](../tests/core-instance-cache.test.js)) | A one-bit change costs one row (2 map lookups, 24 floats, 96 uploaded bytes), not a full collection and a full upload | Two core meshes of one geometry at exactly the same depth may swap which one shows after a flip. Several cameras on one scene flip most rows and cost what a full collection costs. The WebGL2 renderer still uploads every row each frame | Give coincident surfaces a small offset or separate geometries |
| Failed allocations in core (2026-11-07) | By method: `Engine.retain` makes the instance array and the GPU buffers before it changes anything, and `Renderer.add` frees old buffers only after the new ones exist. Covers what throws: the `GPU buffer limit` check, a failed CPU array, `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview`'s GL errors. Proved on a fake device with the real `Engine` and `GPURenderer` ([deep-core-allocation-failure.test.js](../tests/deep-core-allocation-failure.test.js)), and on a real destroyed device in `npm run test:lifecycle:browser` (LIM-330). A failed `rebootDevice` leaves the engine and the canvas on the device they had: the canvas moves last, proved on a real healthy device in the same suite | While a batch grows it holds both sets of buffers, about 1.5 times the new size at the peak. WebGPU reports a real out-of-memory from `createBuffer` asynchronously, not as a throw | A real out-of-memory shows as a `gpu-lost` error on the next frame, with no rollback | Size geometry to the device's `maxBufferSize`; retry a failed `setGeometry` after freeing memory |
| `Picking.pickMany` points per call | Staging memory: 768 bytes a point, freed when the call ends ([picking.ts](../packages/selection/src/picking.ts)). No enforced count. | One 3 x 3 tile a point at WebGPU's 256-byte row pitch. All points read the scene at the call's turn, where separate `engine.pick` calls each read it at their own. | Memory use during a call grows with the number of points, 768 bytes each, until the call ends. | Split a very large list into several calls. |
| Shader variants per engine | Enforced: 64 cached pipeline variants ([renderer.ts](../packages/core/src/renderer.ts)). How close real scenes come: not measured. | Bounds pipeline compilation and memory. Variants come from MSAA, target format and shader text; each pick shader text (`engine.pick` with the scene's pass hooks) is one more. | `RangeError: Shader limit: 64`. | Not needed so far; fewer distinct shader patches per engine. |
| Biome world streaming (`@margoengine/biomes/view`) | Enforced by the check `packages/biomes/tests/flythrough-check.mjs` (run by `check:merge`): a 300 km/h flight over the zero-config world, tiles made by 4 workers as the camera goes, may add at most 0.3 ms to the slowest 1 percent of frames and 1 ms to the worst frame against the same flight with every tile made first; the page spends at most `budget` (default 0.25 ms) a frame sending jobs and copying tiles in. Tile jobs reuse their working arrays: placing the next tile makes 2.1 MB of fresh arrays (24.0 MB before) and a view tile 0.2 MB (4.6 MB before), and a tile's view and placement jobs share one world tile instead of making it twice (`packages/biomes/tests/tile-memory.test.js`). Measured on the RTX A6000 desktop, Edge 156: p99 +0.20 ms, worst +0.00 ms; 111 tiles needed in a flight, 2 arrive after the camera needs them, tile latency p99 337 to 348 ms. On the coordinator's laptop (Ryzen 7 7735HS with a Radeon 680M, 4 workers), three runs from a cool start at the landed code: p99 +0.1, +0.0 and -0.3 ms, worst +0.3, +0.9 and +0.6 ms (before these fixes: p99 +0.3 to +0.6 ms, worst up to +1.8 ms); its prefetched flights themselves vary from run to run (p50 0.8 to 1.4 ms), so a negative figure is that variation, not a gain. | Workers that threw away megabytes of fresh memory per tile slowed the page's own frames on a laptop APU (Ryzen 7 7735HS with a Radeon 680M: cores share memory and power) and failed the check there (p99 +0.3 to +0.6 ms). The fixes on that laptop: a frame sends the jobs it plans within its budget and a frame that plans leaves sending and copying to the next; a send starts only when the budget left covers what a send that reached a worker took lately (a job that only waits in the pool's queue costs nothing and does not count), while copying goes on while budget is left; terrain tiles go in a band of rows at a time; objects have scatter slots for every tile a view keeps (the laptop once ran out of them: `ScatterTiles has no free slot`). The plan of a still camera comes 30 frames after the last plan, not every 30th frame (it once fell right after a plan of the moving camera, and that second plan streamed too: 1 run in 5 failed the plan-frames check); three cool runs with that fix: p99 +0.1, +0.1 and +0.2 ms, worst +0.8, +0.8 and +0.3 ms. The landed code (b8210cd3), three runs: 2 of 3 pass; run 1 p99 +0.1, worst +0.6 ms; run 2 p99 +0.1, worst +1.0 ms, exactly at the limit; run 3 fails: p99 +0.4 ms against 0.3, worst +0.4 ms; every plan, send and packing line was clean in all three. Counting all runs of this streaming code on that laptop, 8 of 9 pass. The one miss is 0.1 ms (one timer step) over the p99 limit, in a run whose streamed flights had fewer frames (703 to 1,083 against about 1,150 to 1,200). On a 680M integrated GPU the margin is thin and the check can miss by one timer step; on the RTX A6000 it passes with p99 +0.10 to +0.20 ms. The limits were not loosened. Figures are medians of three flights per kind. Every worker still runs at once: a fixed cap of half the workers was tried and dropped, it made tiles late on that laptop and cost fast machines late tiles too. | Each world keeps its tile working arrays and each placement its candidate tables between tiles (about 15 MB per worker at the default 256 m tiles) until disposed. The view entry is 7,514 B gzip, over its earlier 7,374 B quality budget; up to 7,516 B accepted by Scott 2026-10-29. | `workers` on `BiomeWorld.create`; `budget`, `lookahead` and `radius` on `BiomeView.attach`; `view.prefetch(rect)` before a planned flight. |

| Biome objects beyond `radius` (`@margoengine/biomes/view`) | Stored trees, shrubs, rocks and props are drawn only for tiles within `radius` (default 1,000 m) of the camera, and grass and other detail within `detailRadius` (default 120 m). | Biome root entry and GPU backend (`@margoengine/biomes`, accepted difference in size, Scott 2026-11-05) | Measured with `npm run quality -- --gate=sizes` (2026-11-05): root 16,329 B gzip, 553 B over its old 15,776 B budget and 329 B over the spec's 16,000 B; the GPU kernels are the lazy `@margoengine/biomes/gpu` entry, 21,714 B (14,425 B before it also took the flow and placement kernels a backend `'gpu'` world routes `hydrologyOfAsync` and `BiomePlacement` through), which only a world that may compute on a device downloads. | Biome worker file (`dist/workers/biomes.js`) | 39,090 B gzip at level 9 and 103,858 B raw (2026-11-08, batch 64; 48,403 B gzip and 129,928 B raw with every optional part inside, commit d04991dda; 51,332 B and 141,164 B before that), against the design's first estimate of about 18 kB. The optional parts are files of their own beside it, each run by a worker with `importScripts` only when its world uses the part, from URLs the page resolves with `new URL(..., import.meta.url)` (so the app's bundler copies them) and sends with each replica's first message: `biomes-splines.js` 4,245 B, `biomes-erosion.js` 2,557 B, `biomes-graph.js` 2,952 B, `biomes-zones.js` 1,790 B and `biomes-multinoise.js` 2,142 B (gzip level 9). The worker build ([build-workers.js](../scripts/build-workers.js)) swaps the GPU, digest and presets entries for an empty stub ([worker-empty-stub.js](../scripts/worker-empty-stub.js)): a worker's world never gets a device, no worker job makes a digest, and the page sends its world's biomes, so the replica never needs the default ones. It resolves the package's own entries to their sources, and a part reads every module it shares with the worker from the worker's copy, so the six files hold one copy of each module (and each hook one object); `packages/biomes/tests/workers.test.js` counts one copy of the integer helpers, each part's code in its own file only and none of the digest or presets code, and measures the worker. Lazy: only a world created with `workers` loads it, and it counts toward no entry's budget. | A worker runs the whole tile path by itself: world, region, relief, placement, cover and the view's tile functions. Reaching about 18 kB would also take placement, the view and cover tile functions out, which every view with objects needs, so the worker would do less of the tile. The worker keeps every export of the modules its parts share, about 940 B gzip over a trial build without the parts (38,153 B). | A world with `workers` downloads the worker file once and each part it uses once; every worker shares the browser's copies. | Leave `workers` off and tiles are made on the page's thread. |
| Biome rivers (`@margoengine/biomes/view`) | Fixed for v1.0.0: river and lake water stands still (`water: { rivers: 'auto' }` or `'hydrology'`, 1.5 m over the bed, falling with it; `lakes: 'auto'` at the hydrology's fill level); it does not flow. | Biome settlements (`@margoengine/biomes/settlements`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `villages` and `sites` at most 64, `houses` at most 256 a village, `spacing` 50 to 100,000 m, `cell` 2 to 256 m and at most 4,194,304 grid cells, `maxGrade` 0.02 to 1, `siteGrade` 0.005 to 1, `bridge` 1 to 1,000, `detour` 1 to 100, `yard` 0 to 100 m. Measured (diagnostic, Node on the busy Beelink): about 1.4 s for the default 4 km world at the 16 m cell, three villages (LIM-524). | Roads are least-cost paths on the site grid, one A* search a link, so the layout reads the ground once a cell and its time grows with the cells and the links; a finer `cell` follows the ground more closely at the square of the cost. | Roads bend at grid cells (thinned to 0.75 of a cell, then a Catmull-Rom curve), so on a 16 m cell a road can cut a tight valley's corner by a few metres; houses are rectangles on straight lanes, with no building mesh; a village on hilly relief gets fewer than `houses` lots (each lot must be level within `siteGrade`); rivers count only where `rivers` lines say, and a road never crosses the sea. | Pass `sites` to place villages yourself, a smaller `cell` for closer roads, a larger `siteGrade` for terraced lots, or your own paths to /splines. |
| Biome placement graphs (`@margoengine/biomes/graph`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: 1 to 256 nodes; ids of letters, digits, `_` and `-`; `multiply`, `min`, `max` and `add` take 2 to 16 inputs; curves 2 to 16 points with x increasing; noise `scale` 1 to 100,000 whole metres; every value 0..1; no cycle; every output selector selects a species of the world. | Biome ecosystem growth (`@margoengine/biomes/ecosystem`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: 0 to 2,000 years; 1 to 1,000,000 plants held (default 200,000; seedlings past it are counted in `crowded`); crowns 0.1 to 40 m; 0 to 64 seedlings per adult a year; dispersal scale 0.5 to 2,000 m, capped at 30 scales; bounds and plants within 100 km of the origin. By method: every year rebuilds a crown grid and tests each plant against the crowns of its 3 x 3 cells, so a cost that grows with plants times neighbours times years. | Frame allocation (JavaScript heap per steady-state frame) | Measured by the check `npm run test:frame-alloc:browser` ([frame-alloc-browser.mjs](../scripts/frame-alloc-browser.mjs), scenes in [tests/fixtures/frame-alloc](../tests/fixtures/frame-alloc/main.js); run by `check:merge`). RTX A6000 desktop, Edge 156 headless with `--enable-precise-memory-info`: `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize` read once per frame, 600 warm-up frames (one of them, 60 before recording, late on purpose: a 200 ms stall, so the floors hold for the steady state after a late frame) then 600 recorded, frames with a garbage collection left out, the median frame, largest of three runs, at the item 53.1 commit (`perf(core, shadows, post)`, 2026-10-29). Per frame, before and after (two steps, item 53.1 parts 1 and 2): three lit meshes 1,428 B to 340 B; 10,000 moving instanced boxes 1,076 B to 292 B; the same room with cascaded shadows and eight moving casters 26,920 B to 860 B; with SSAO, Bloom, tone mapping and FXAA 5,116 B to 1,528 B. The room plus 10,000 `DynamicInstances` boxes (@margoengine/culling), every row rewritten each frame through bulk writes and `update()`, measured 396 B in three runs at the item 53.2 commit (56 B over the room alone, among them the 16 B wrapper of its compute pass). The check fails when a median frame passes these floors; they are only ever lowered. | Every byte a frame allocates is a byte the garbage collector must sweep later, and a collection in the middle of a frame is a stutter. Margo reuses its arrays, descriptors and callbacks from frame to frame instead of making new ones. | Not 0 B, and it cannot reach 0 B: every WebGPU call that returns an object (the command encoder and its finished command buffer, each render pass, the canvas's current texture and its view) hands back a new 16 B JavaScript wrapper from the browser, and V8 stores the fractional frame time it passes to frame callbacks and plugins as a heap number. Shadows and post-processing add passes, so they add wrappers. Measured and left as they are: the frame-resources view set clears about 120 B per frame in the post scene (a fix changes the protocol between copies of the resources, judged risky for a frozen core), the SSAO scene walk makes an iterator and an options literal, the fixture setters box about 216 B in the shadowed scene, and each returned WebGPU object costs 16 B. Number boxing in V8's middle tier (Maglev) is gated too: `tests/frame-alloc.test.js` fails a core frame over 780 B, shadows over 620 B and the cascade fit over 128 B there on V8 14 (Node 26) and newer. V8 13 (Node 24, the minimum Node) passes the core limit (628 B) but its Maglev calls Math.sqrt with a boxed argument and result, 32 B a call, so it has its own row for the other two: shadows over 1,120 B (measured 1,081 B, 704 B of it 22 square roots) and the cascade fit over 256 B (measured 242 B, 224 B of it 7 square roots); a square root in JavaScript arithmetic with the same bits would cost every engine more time. Node 22 has no Maglev by default, so the middle-tier probes skip there. A late frame once deoptimized core's frame loop (its delta clamp first ran a compare on a frame past `maxDelta`, with no type feedback), and the loop then ran its next thousands of frames in a tier that boxes numbers: 24 to 84 B more per frame in every scene, seen only when `check:merge` loaded the machine. Fixed in core, and gated twice: the browser check's late warm-up frame, and `tests/frame-alloc.test.js`, which fails when a late frame leaves the loop unoptimized. The Node probes compile on the main thread (`--no-concurrent-recompilation`), so a package build running beside them cannot make them measure a lower tier. `npm run test:frame-alloc:nodes` runs the test on every Node it finds; the probes leave out windows in which V8 collected garbage. In these runs 0 to 3 of 600 recorded frames held a collection. | Keep your own `onFrame` callbacks allocation-free (the check's scenes keep their clock in a `Float64Array`). `node scripts/frame-alloc-browser.mjs --profile --source` names the functions that allocate per frame. |

| Far voxel levels (`@margoengine/voxel/lod`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: 1 to 12 levels, `radius` 2 to 32 nodes, `scale` a power of two to 4,096. By method: a level-L cell is 2^L blocks, so detail under a cell is gone (a tree, a one-block wall) and a coarse surface is within half a cell of the real one; `noiseTerrainLod` leaves out caves and trees; edits to the real world show in far levels only where its chunks are loaded; nodes generate on the main thread, `budget` a frame; the streamed chunks must stay inside level 1 (`2 * radius` above the streamer's `distance` + 1) or the two overlap; while a level changes, old and new nodes may both show for a few frames; a scaled renderer takes no lighting effects, shadows or capture. Frame cost at kilometre views is unmeasured. | Each far level is a coarser copy of the world, so it cannot hold detail finer than its cells. | Trees and one-block walls are gone in far levels, and old and new nodes may both show for a few frames while a level changes. | Pass your own `generate` function (`VoxelLodOptions.generate`) to put trees or walls into far cells; `noiseTerrainLod` is only one generator and leaves them out. |
| Voxel light in a worker (`@margoengine/voxel/light-worker`, 2026-11-07) | By method: the worker holds a second copy of every loaded chunk's blocks and light; the page still packs each loaded chunk once and copies the light of changed chunks back (32 KiB each); one worker per world, not with `VoxelLighting` on the same world. | Light is worked out in a worker on its own copy of the chunks. | Light arrives a frame or more after a change. | Use `VoxelLighting.attach(world)` on the page instead: it keeps no second copy of the chunks, but its flood fill runs on the page thread. |
| Coloured block light (`@margoengine/voxel/light-rgb`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: colours 0..1, `extent` multiples of 32 up to 1,024. By method: three copies of every loaded chunk (blocks and light) and three floods per change; coloured light only inside the box around the camera (default 128 x 64 x 128 blocks); not on scaled renderers. | Coloured light keeps three copies of every loaded chunk and floods three times per change, so it is limited to a box around the camera. | A level is rounded per channel, so dim colours lose hue. | The renderer's own block light should be switched off (`blockLightColor` [0, 0, 0]) or it adds on top. |
| Flowing liquids (`@margoengine/voxel/fluids`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `reach` 1 to 7, `delay` 1 or more, at most `maxUpdates` cells a tick and 10 ticks an update. | By method: levels in eighths (state data), so a liquid runs at most 7 cells from a source; | flow toward drops looks 4 cells ahead; no currents pushing bodies, no pressure (a liquid never rises); unloaded chunks stop it like rock; speed on large pools unmeasured. | Place further sources to carry a liquid past 7 cells (`infinite: true` makes two neighbouring sources renew one); `maxUpdates` caps the cells updated a tick on large pools. |
| Block ticks (`@margoengine/voxel/ticks`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `randomTicks` 0 to 4,096 a chunk, at most `maxUpdates` scheduled and neighbour updates a tick, 10 ticks an update. | By method: changes made by hooks run next tick (no recursion), so a chain of falling blocks moves one cell per tick plus its delay; random ticks cost every loaded chunk every tick; falling blocks are cells, not bodies. | A chain of falling blocks moves one cell per tick plus its delay, and random ticks cost every loaded chunk every tick. | Lower `randomTicks` (default 24 a chunk, 0 to 4,096) to cut random tick cost, and pass a smaller `delay` to `fallingRule(delay)` (default 2, 1 or more) to speed a falling chain. |
| Voxel GPU meshing (`@margoengine/voxel/gpu-mesher`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `batch` 1 to 32 chunks and within the device's storage binding limit (about 3.2 MB of scratch per chunk). By method: chunks with a slab or stair within a cell are meshed on the page; the page still packs each chunk and its shell and flood-fills visibility; two GPU round trips per batch; each slice's greedy merge runs in one invocation, so the GPU path is not faster than `meshChunk` on the M6 Mac mini; one block table per batch. | Chunks with a slab or stair within a cell are meshed on the page, and each slice's greedy merge runs in one invocation. | The GPU path is not faster than `meshChunk` on the M6 Mac mini. | Leave out the `mesher` option of `VoxelRenderer.attach`: its default worker pool meshes with `meshChunk`, which is no slower here. |
| Smooth voxel terrain (`@margoengine/voxel/smooth`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: densities clamped to -1..1 in 1/127ths, materials 0 to 255, sculpt radius up to 64 and strength -2 to 2, chunk y within `minChunkY` to `maxChunkY`. By method: meshing runs on the page thread (`budget` chunks a frame); no relaxation pass, so the surface keeps a slight cell pattern; one core mesh per chunk and material, plain colour materials (no textures or triplanar mapping); no far levels; past an unloaded neighbour the surface is left open; smooth terrain has no collision with `@margoengine/voxel/physics`. | Meshing runs on the page thread, one core mesh is made per chunk and material, and the surface has no relaxation pass. | A slight cell pattern on the surface, an open surface past an unloaded neighbour, and no collision with `@margoengine/voxel/physics`. | Set `budget` on `SmoothTerrainView` (default 4 chunks an `update()`) to spread meshing over frames, and load the neighbouring chunks to close the surface; `meshSmoothChunk` returns each chunk's positions and indices if you build a collider of your own. |
| Voxel bounce light (`@margoengine/voxel/gi`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `strength` 0 to 8, `softness` 0 to 0.5 rad, `cells` 4,096 to 262,144, `rays` 1 to 16, `range` 4 to 64. By method: a 64 x 64 x 64 cell window around the camera; one bounce of sunlight (no sky, block light or multi-bounce); only opaque cubes stop rays and bounce (slabs, stairs, leaves, glass and liquids pass light); light per cell, L1 spherical harmonics, so detail finer than a cell and sharp shadow edges are lost; light settles over several updates after a change; noisy with few `rays`; not on scaled renderers. | Light is kept per cell in a 64 x 64 x 64 window around the camera, as L1 spherical harmonics, and each update traces a few rays. | Detail finer than a cell and sharp shadow edges are lost, light settles over several updates after a change, and few `rays` look noisy. | Raise `rays` for less noise. |
| Voxel destruction (`@margoengine/voxel/debris`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `maxCells` 1 to 65,536 (default 4,096: a bigger joined group stays as if held), `maxPieces` 1 or more (default 64), `lifetime` > 0 s, `density` > 0. By method: only removals of solid blocks start a search, on the page thread at `update()`; an unloaded chunk counts as holding; pieces are whole cubes for collider and mesh (slabs and stairs too), flat colour without the world's textures or light, and never go back into the world; non-solid blocks resting on a piece (flowers) stay where they were. | The search after an edit stops at a holding cell or `maxCells`, and a piece is built from whole cells in flat colour so it costs one body and one mesh per block type. | A loose group of `maxCells` blocks or more stays hanging, an overhang into an unloaded chunk stays up, and a falling slab looks like a full block without its texture. | Raise `maxCells` (up to 65,536) for larger pieces, load the neighbouring chunks before cutting, and pass `material` for your own look. |
| Voxel-edit shader brushes (`@margoengine/voxel-edit/shaders`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: 1 to 1,024 passes, up to 16 params, a 256-entry table of 0 to 255, values clamped to 255, a grid (and tool) within the device's storage binding limit (128 MiB by default) and `maxCells` (default 16,777,216). By method: every cell of a pass reads the grid as it was before that pass; one submit per pass; the whole grid is uploaded and read back per `run`; brushes see one grid and one tool grid. | Grids are packed four cells to a word in one storage binding, and the CPU builds the selection mask and counts changed cells. | A grid larger than the binding limit is refused, and each `run` pays an upload and a read-back. | Split a large model into tiles with `voxTiles` (`./vox`) and brush each. |
| Voxel-edit rigs (`@margoengine/voxel-edit/rig`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: unit quaternions (length within 0.001 of 1), unique bone names with parents listed first, parts on known bones, a baked box within `maxCells` (default 16,777,216). By method: each part follows one bone rigidly; a bake gives each cell the part cell under its centre, later parts over earlier ones. | Blocky characters move whole parts; blending cells between bones would tear the grid. | Turns other than quarter turns resample, so a turned part keeps its cell count only roughly; parts do not bend. | Use quarter turns for exact frames; for smooth skinning mesh the parts and use `@margoengine/rigging` with `@margoengine/animation`. |
| Voxel-edit GPU bulk edits (`@margoengine/voxel-edit/gpu`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: a grid within the device's storage binding limit (128 MiB by default) and `maxCells` (default 16,777,216, at most 67,108,864); fill radius 0 to 128; 0 to 1,024 iterations per filter; a 256-entry remap table of 0 to 255; a brush made on the grid's own device. By method: every edit reads the grid as the edit before left it; one submit per pass; a combine uploads its tool grid each time and counts clipped cells on the CPU. | Exact integer cell work keeps every result equal to the CPU operation. | A grid larger than one storage binding is refused, not split. | Split a large model with `voxTiles` (`./vox`) and edit each tile. |
| Voxel-edit shared editing (`@margoengine/voxel-edit/collab`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: a site name of 1 to 256 characters, 65,535 sites per replica, clock and seq 1 to 4,294,967,295, cells inside the grid, values 0 to 255, `maxCells` (default 16,777,216). By method: each cell keeps the write with the highest Lamport clock, the higher site name breaking a tie; an operation already applied is ignored. | Last writer wins per cell needs no server and no conflict step, and merges in any order. | Each cell keeps one value, so two users drawing over the same cells keep only the later stroke; a replica keeps 7 bytes a cell plus every operation seen (5 bytes per edited cell), with no compaction. | Start a new shared grid from a snapshot when the log grows too large; give each user a stable site name. |
| Goxel and VoxEdit files (`@margoengine/voxel-edit/formats`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `.gox` versions 1 and 2 read, 2 written; BL16 blocks of exactly 64 x 64 pixels; at most 4,096 layers; `maxCells` (default 16,777,216) counts each layer's block bounds before cropping; names and dictionary values written up to 255 bytes. `.vxm` versions 3 to 13 read, 12 written; at most 255 materials (palette indices 1 to 255) and 255 models, all of one size; textures up to 2,048 and face lists up to 262,144 quads are skipped, larger ones refused. By method: from a clean-room specification, not from either program. | Neither format has a public specification; the one Margo reads was written from two programs' behaviour and eight sample files, and lists what it could not determine. | Skipped and lost on a round trip: `.gox` cameras, light, preview, material lists beyond one default on writing, layer matrices of plain layers (written as identity), and the fork-only PLAC, CLRH and CUST chunks; `.vxm` baked meshes, textures, surface data, palette chunks and the trailer. Unknown and so not checked: the `.gox` chunk CRC (no writer computes one; written as 0), the colour space of block colours, the meaning of alpha 1 to 254 (read as solid), clone layers under a rotating `mat` (each voxel centre goes to the cell it lands in), and the inside test at a shape's exact edge (centres on the edge count as inside); `.vxm` versions other than 4 and 12 (no sample files; version 13 in particular rests on one program's reader), the v6 to v10 texture compression, the pivot X convention of v10 and older (returned as stored), and whether VoxEdit opens a file with no baked mesh, as `writeVXM` writes. | Open a written `.vxm` in VoxEdit before relying on it; keep `.vox` (`./vox`) as the exchange file when a model must keep cameras, materials or meshes. |
| Voxel-net entities (`@margoengine/voxel-net/entities`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `maxEntities` (default 4,096, at most 1,048,576), `maxPerPlayer` (default 256, nearest first), kind 0 to 65,535, state 0 to 255, `leaveRadius` at least `radius` (default 64 and 10% more). By method: entities over a chunk the server has not loaded do not move; each entity is quantized once per tick and sent as a delta against the player's last message; a player away (parked) gets every entity again in full. | Sending only what is near and changed keeps a crowded world within the 20 Hz tick and each link. | A world of many entities steps every one each tick on the server's thread, with no sleeping of far ones beyond unloaded chunks; brains run on the main thread; no pathfinding (only `wander`). | Keep entities near players; write your own brain for chase or flee; raise `maxPerPlayer` with care for the link. |
| Voxel-net shards (`@margoengine/voxel-net/shards`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `regionSize` a multiple of 32 blocks (default 256), `margin` 0 to half the region (default 8), `secret` at least 16 characters, tickets good for `ticketLife` (default 10,000 ms) and once, a handed-off player closed with 4001 after `grace` (default 5,000 ms). Measured on loopback in one process only (two servers, real sockets); not measured between machines. | Each shard is a plain VoxelServer that owns its regions' edits; tickets carry the player across, so no shard needs another's state. | A shard sees only its own edits: the other side of a border shows as generated until the player crosses. A handoff keeps position, not velocity, and lands on the ground; the next shard sends the chunks around the player again. | Put busy areas inside one region; make regions larger than the view distance so borders are crossed rarely. |
| Voxel-net WebTransport (`@margoengine/voxel-net/webtransport`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `inputCopies` 0 to 8 (default 3), the copies of one message at most 120 steps; a gap of more than 240 lost steps closes the client with 1002. Measured over an in-memory stand-in link only (a third of datagrams lost each way, every 5th survivor late): no step lost with 3 copies, client and server within 0.05 blocks. | Inputs are small, so copies cost little and make a lost datagram free; whole snapshots cost more bytes than deltas but need no acknowledgement. | A dropped session is not resumed. The slow-client check does not see a WebTransport stream backing up. Players snapshots go whole, so they are larger than over a WebSocket. | Connect again on close; keep `playerDistance` small for crowded worlds; use a WebSocket where WebTransport is missing. |
| Voxel-net chat and inventory (`@margoengine/voxel-net/chat`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: client app messages at most 16,384 bytes and `appRate` 20 per second (burst 20) per player, the rest dropped; a chat line at most 256 UTF-8 bytes after cleaning, `rate` 1 per second (burst 5); inventories 1 to 1,024 slots (default 36), `stackLimit` default 64. Measured over real sockets on one machine only. | The server owns lines and items, so a client can only say a line or ask to move its own items. | Lines over the rate and moves that are not possible are dropped or answered with the slots as they are. Inventories live in server memory; no chat history for players who join later, no channels or mute lists. | Raise `appRate`, `rate` or `burst`; drop lines with `filter`; save inventories with `slots` and restore them with `load`. |
| Voxel-net lag compensation (`@margoengine/voxel-net/rewind`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `maxRewind` above 0 and at most 4,000 ticks (default 0.5 s); a view tick older is checked `maxRewind` back, a future one now; `maxDistance` default 64 blocks. Measured over real sockets on one machine only, a walker at 2.5 blocks per second. | A client draws others about `interpolationDelay` behind, so without rewinding its aim is behind the target. | A client can claim any view tick up to `maxRewind` back. Blocks are not rewound: one placed since the view tick stops the shot. Shapes blend in a line between ticks, as the client draws them. | Lower `maxRewind` to give a cheat less; pass `hitbox` for heads or capsules; call `shoot` yourself for shots of your own. |
| Voxel-net database store (`@margoengine/voxel-net/sql-store`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `table` letters, digits and `_`, at most 63 characters, optionally after one `schema.` (default `margo_chunks`); chunk coordinates -2^26 to 2^26-1. Tested on `node:sqlite` only; the Postgres SQL runs through SQLite, never against a Postgres server. | A folder with a file per chunk grows past what file systems list and back up well for large worlds. | On SQLite each query runs on the server's thread, so a slow disk stalls ticks. The store cannot list its chunks. | Use a Postgres `Pool` to keep queries off the thread; turn on SQLite WAL (`PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`); one `table` per world. |
| Voxel-net built-in TLS (`@margoengine/voxel-net/server` option `tls`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `tls` needs PEM `key` and `cert` that build a secure context, checked when the server is made and on `setTls`; a TLS handshake must finish within `helloTimeout` (default 3,000 ms). Tested over loopback with a self-signed certificate only. | Small hosts want `wss://` without running a reverse proxy. | `maxPending` and `maxPerAddress` count from the WebSocket upgrade on, so bare TLS handshakes are not capped by them. One certificate per server (no SNI choice between names); no HTTP/2. | A firewall or reverse proxy in front for floods, many names or HTTP/2; `setTls` for renewals; `tls: { ca }` on Node clients for a certificate of your own. |

## Rendering

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One directional light in core | Enforced by design: core's lighting is one direction and one radiance, plus a colourless scalar ambient. | Every light model beyond one sun is an optional package, so apps that need one sun pay for one sun. | No API for a second sun in core; core's own ambient does not light metals. | `@margoengine/clustered`: up to 1,024 point and spot lights (`RangeError: Expected at most 1,024 lights` past that). `@margoengine/clustered/shadows`: shadows for up to 16 of them ([local-shadows-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/local-shadows-gpu.json)). `@margoengine/clustered/area` (8,946 B gzip): up to 64 rectangle area lights (`RangeError: Expected at most 64 area lights`), unshadowed, no texture bindings ([area-lights-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/area-lights-gpu.json)). More directional lights: `@margoengine/clustered/directional` (1,563 B gzip), up to 16 (`RangeError: Expected an array of at most 16 directional lights`), unshadowed. IES profiles: `@margoengine/clustered/ies` (3,697 B gzip), at most 16 distinct profiles, type C files only. Projector spots: `@margoengine/clustered/projector` (2,618 B gzip), at most 16 images of up to 4,096 texels a side. Physical units: `@margoengine/clustered/units` (833 B gzip). All three light entries use storage buffers, no texture bindings ([light-features-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/light-features-gpu.json)). Configurable ambient: `@margoengine/environment` `HemisphereLight` and `AmbientLight`, one per engine. Image-based lighting: `@margoengine/environment`. |
| 16 sampled textures and 16 samplers per shader stage | Enforced by WebGPU's guaranteed minimum; Margo's device asks for no more. gltf-pro's physical material with directional shadows, IBL and local shadows uses exactly 16 (asserted in [instancing.test.js](../packages/gltf-pro/tests/instancing.test.js)). | Every adapter, phones included, supports 16. Requiring more would make the same app fail on some devices. | A `RangeError` naming the combination, e.g. `gltf-pro: physical material + shadows + environment:lighting + clustered + clustered:shadows + shader patch needs 17 sampled textures per shader stage; this device allows 16`. | Drop one lighting feature for that material, or use the standard material (8 of 16 with everything attached). `VolumetricFog`, SSAO, clustered lights, area lights and light probes (`@margoengine/environment/probes`: one storage buffer; with an environment fallback they take EnvironmentLighting's place and its bindings) add no textures. Texture arrays are planned after 1.0. |
| float32 coordinates | Measured on the GPU ([large-coordinates-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/large-coordinates-gpu.json), 10 mm part, camera 50 mm away): core alone jitters 0.38 px at 1 km and 42 px at 100 km; at 6,000 km the part is not drawn. Per-stage CPU breakdown in [large-coordinates.md](large-coordinates.md). | Core and its kernel store positions and matrices in float32: half the memory and bandwidth of float64, and the format GPUs consume. | No error. Parts shake while the camera moves, small features collapse, specular shifts (2.8° at 100 km), and far enough out geometry disappears. | `FloatingOrigin` in `@margoengine/cameras/origin` (1,258 B gzip, 0 core bytes): 0.019 px jitter at every distance up to 6,000 km, and `engine.pick` hits the part at every distance ([large-coordinates.md](large-coordinates.md#the-plugin)). Vertices or child offsets that are already kilometres from their root inside one asset must be re-centred at export. |
| Transparency | Default: transparent materials and gltf-pro `BLEND` primitives are sorted back to front per mesh; core meshes are opaque. Measured ([oit-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/oit-gpu.json), a 50 % housing over gears orbited 360 × 1°): 13 steps with more than 1 % of covered pixels popping. | Sorting is exact for separate objects and needs no extra targets. | Popping where transparent parts interpenetrate or nest, as the camera moves. | `@margoengine/oit` (2,210 B gzip): 0 popping steps on the same orbit. Weighted blended OIT is an approximation: colour error against exact blending 0.5 / 4.6 / 8.7 (0-255) for 1 / 2 / 4 layers. Transmission and custom blending keep the sorted path unless `blending` is set; limits in its [README](../packages/oit/README.md#limits-the-wboit-approximation). |
| Screen-space reflections | Enforced by method: only what is on screen reflects. Core meshes and models passed to `ssr.add(model)` (gltf-pro, materials, terrain, water) show reflections; other custom shaders are reflected but do not reflect. Cost measured on a worst-case glossy floor ([ssr-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/ssr-gpu.json), quiet-gated): 2.2-2.3 ms at 1280×720, 5.8-5.9 ms at 1920×1080. | Reusing depth and colour that are already rendered avoids a second scene pass. Each custom pipeline needs its own capture into SSR's targets. | Reflections fade at screen edges and miss off-screen objects (reflection probes fill in where attached); water and terrain not added keep their own sky reflection. | `@margoengine/post/ssr` (9,068 B gzip) is itself the opt-in. Off-screen reflections: reflection probes in `@margoengine/environment/probes`; SSR removes the probes' own specular only where its ray hits on screen and keeps the probe's reflection elsewhere ([probes-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/probes-gpu.json): off screen the floor equals the frame without SSR, 95th percentile 0/255). Limits in the [post README](../packages/post/README.md). |
| Volumetric fog | Enforced by design: one froxel grid (default 160 × 90 × 64) whatever the screen size, so shadow edges in the fog are about one froxel wide (8 × 8 px at 1280 × 720). Effects measured in [volumetric-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/volumetric-gpu.json). | A froxel volume makes light shafts follow real shadows at a fixed cost per frame. | Particles, VFX, splats and transparent surfaces are fogged only when added with `fog.add` (additive, multiply and transmission surfaces never); nothing beyond `range`; local fog volumes only from `/fog-volumes`; multiple scattering (`multipleScattering`) is a per-froxel estimate: it follows the froxel's own sun shadow, clustered lights add none, and f is capped at 0.95. Errors: `RangeError: Volumetric grid exceeds device limit`; `VolumetricFog replaces environment Fog '<name>': set its enabled = false or remove it`; `VolumetricFog needs scene depth: attach a post capture (Tonemap, Bloom, PostStack, SSAO, TAA) first or pass options.depth`. | `@margoengine/environment/volumetric` (6,923 B gzip) is itself the opt-in: a finer `grid` sharpens edges at a higher cost; `fog.texture` lets custom shaders (particles) sample the fog. Limits in the [environment README](../packages/environment/README.md). |
| Light probes (indirect light) | Enforced ([probes.ts](../packages/environment/src/probes.ts), [probes.test.js](../packages/environment/tests/probes.test.js)): one irradiance volume of at most 4,096 L1/L2 probes (64 per axis) and at most 16 box-projected reflection probes per `LightProbes`. The volume is baked; reflection probes are baked or captured live a few cube faces per frame (`setLive`; a moved box shows in a 128 px probe 7-11 frames later at one face per frame, capture GPU time per frame 0.066 ms or less and a median 0.20 ms on the prefilter frame, RTX A6000, [probes-live-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/probes-live-gpu.json)). Measured bake of 8 volume probes and one 128 px reflection probe 114-121 ms (diagnostic: other jobs running; [probes-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/probes-gpu.json)). Accuracy in the same file: volume SH within 1.7% of DC against an analytic room. | Baking turns the scene's light into lookups (no ray tracing per frame) and keeps them in one storage buffer, so no texture binding is spent. | Volume light stays as baked until `bake()` runs again; live reflection probes lag the scene by up to (probes + 1) refreshes of 6 / `facesPerFrame` frames and see only what the frame draws (render with `culling: false`); light leaks through walls thinner than the probe spacing (no visibility per probe); mirror-sharp reflections show texel-sized steps near wall edges at the default 128 px. Errors: `RangeError: Invalid irradiance volume: min < max, 1-64 probes per axis (4,096 in total), sh 1 or 2, blend >= 0`, `RangeError: Expected at most 16 reflection probes`, `RangeError: Light probe buffer exceeds device limit`, `light-probes replaces EnvironmentLighting: pass {environment} to LightProbes instead of attaching both`. | `@margoengine/environment/probes` (14,984 B gzip) is itself the opt-in: re-bake on demand or capture reflections live, one volume box per room against leaks, a finer `resolution` for sharper reflections. Dynamic GI: none yet. |
| Plugins in probe captures (`LightProbes.addCapture`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: a plugin with `registerPasses`; `passes`, when given, names passes it registers; at least one pass to replay. By method: the passes replay into every probe face with the face's context, and those ordered before the capture run again with the frame's context; on an Apple M6 (Metal) terrain and a sky show in a baked probe (LIM-644). | Terrain, sky and any plugin that draws from the context's camera show in reflections and the bounce light with no capture code of their own. | Water throws in a probe face (it reads the frame's viewport-sized scene depth); VFX particles would draw the frame's view (their camera is uploaded by the simulation pass); replayed passes draw their own fog; a pass that advances a simulation must not be named. Errors: `TypeError: LightProbes addCapture needs a plugin with registerPasses()`, `RangeError: LightProbes addCapture: <name> has no pass '<pass>'`. | Draw water and particles into probes once their packages draw from the context's camera; until then leave them out of the capture (the environment fills in). |
| Tiled EXR (`parseTiledEXR`, `@margoengine/environment/exr-tiled`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: single-part tiled files with NONE, RLE, ZIPS, ZIP or PIZ, one level, mipmaps or ripmaps, either rounding mode; every tile is placed by its own chunk header, so any tile order reads; a tile decodes to at most 256 MiB and the requested levels to at most 2 x 2^26 pixels; scanline files go to `parseEXR`. By method: a tile is decoded as a scanline block as wide as the tile (LIM-647). | Studio tools' tiled and mipmapped EXR textures load, with every level when asked. | PXR24, B44, B44A, DWAA and DWAB are refused here (no byte-level description to build a clean-room decoder from); `decodeEXR` in `/exr-codecs` reads them and the full-resolution level of tiled files through the prebuilt OpenEXR worker. Deep, multi-part and subsampled files are refused as by `parseEXR`. Errors: `MargoError unsupported: Unsupported EXR compression <name>: OpenEXR publishes no byte-level description of it ...`, `MargoError failed: Invalid EXR: tile <i> has bad coordinates`, `RangeError: Invalid EXR: tiles are too small for the image size`. |
| Ambient diffuse under `KHR_materials_specular` | Enforced by method ([ibl.ts](../packages/environment/src/ibl.ts)): direct light and `Transmission` weight the base by one number, `1 - max(F)`, as the spec writes it. The split-sum ambient hooks (`EnvironmentLighting`, `LightProbes`, sky) keep what the specular term leaves per channel, so a coloured `specularColorFactor` tints their diffuse slightly. | The spec's scalar would change partly metallic texels of every plain material. | A faint complement tint on diffuse light from an environment, only with a coloured specular. | Light the surface directly, or use a grey specular colour. |
| Environment blend (`@margoengine/environment/blend`, 2026-11-07) | By method: a linear crossfade of two environments' radiance, `(1 - t) x from + t x to`, in the source cube, every prefiltered specular mip and the SH; on an Apple M6 (Metal) every texel of every mip equals the weighted sources within 3 x 2^-11 relative (rgba16float rounding of two inputs and the output; worst seen 9.5e-4) and a quarter-turned source lands texel for texel (LIM-493). | Ground projected environment (`@margoengine/environment/ground`, 2026-11-08) | By method: per pixel the view ray meets the floor plane at `center`'s height or the dome (a sphere of `radius`), and the environment is read along the direction from the photo camera (`height` above `center`) to that point; on an Apple M6 (Metal) every pixel from two cameras equals a CPU mirror of that geometry within 0.15% and a floor point seen from the second camera keeps its colour within 0.13% (a plain background: over 3x) (LIM-498). `height` above 0 and below `radius`, `radius` finite, `center` three finite numbers. | Exact analytic geometry in the background's fragment shader; no extra pass. | The floor is flat and the dome a sphere, so walls and objects in the photo bend as the camera moves; the camera must stay inside the dome and above the floor; no contact shadow; cost not timed. | Pick `height` as the photo's tripod height; add `@margoengine/shadows` for contact shadows. |
| Dynamic global illumination (`DynamicGI` in `@margoengine/environment/gi`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: 1 to 64 probes per axis and at most 4,096, `probesPerFrame` 1 to 4,096, `resolution` a power of two 8 to 64. | Probe visibility (`volume.visibility` in `@margoengine/environment/probes`, 2026-11-08) | By method: 24 direction bins per probe (cube face by quadrant) of mean and mean square distance, capped at 1.5 cell diagonals; Chebyshev visibility cubed and a smooth backface term per probe, renormalised. | Sphere and blended reflection probes (`shape: 'sphere'`, `reflectionBlend: 'weighted'` in `@margoengine/environment/probes`, 2026-11-08) | By method: a sphere probe's parallax point is the far hit of the reflected ray with its sphere and its fade runs past the surface; weighted blending sums probes by fade weight, normalised past 1; on an Apple M6 (Metal) both match a CPU mirror within 3.2e-7 at 512 random rays (LIM-549). | No cost without them (box probes in order keep their shader text); a sphere adds one ray-sphere solve per probe per fragment. | Spheres are centred where they are created; capture still sees through each probe's own position only; cost not timed. | Use spheres for round or open areas and weighted blending where probes overlap at a doorway or a clearing. |

Proved on one GPU, a Radeon 680M (LIM-386). | The lift moves each vertex by the snow depth where its own normal faces up, so it follows vertices. | A mesh whose faces share no vertices, such as a `box()`, opens a slit along its top edges, and a coarse mesh drifts coarsely. | Use smooth meshes with shared normals, which stay closed, or lower `depth` (0 to 2 m), since the slit is as deep as the snow; `snowWGSL` is the shader for your own materials. |
| Spatial weather regions (`@margoengine/weather/regions`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: front speed 0 to 200 m/s and width 1 to 100,000 m; cell radius 1 to 1,000,000 m. | Authoring shapes, not a forecast model (LIM-388). | By method: fronts are straight lines at a constant speed and cells are circles at a constant velocity, blended in a fixed order (base, fronts, cells), so there is no front that bends, stalls or occludes and no cell that grows from the air; a place's ground wetness and snow come from the machine it feeds, not from the map's history there. | Stack several `fronts` and `cells` (`addFront`, `addCell`; they apply in order over the base), and give a cell `life: [from, to]` to grow it in and fade it out. |
| Hail lighting and splashes (`lit` and `splashes` on `@margoengine/weather/hail`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `splashes` 0 to 8 chips a stone. | By method: a stone is shaded as a ball from its place across its streak by the engine's one sun and ambient light, Lambert diffuse and a Blinn-Phong glint: it casts no shadow and the scene's shadows do not reach it, so a stone under a roof is lit as in the open; chips burst from the ground height `groundY`, not from the surface the stone meets, and fly on closed-form paths without colliding. | Weather drive (`@margoengine/weather/drive`, 2026-11-07) | By method: it writes numbers into targets each frame before they draw; it sets a sky's cloud sheet and fog only when the sky has them, and cloud cover is the state's `cloud` for every layer (no cloud types or heights from the weather); the layer's density (0.02 to 0.08 per metre) and its wind aloft (three times the ground wind) are design choices, not measured profiles. | Weather audio cues (`@margoengine/weather/audio`, 2026-11-07) | By method: the rain and wind are one looping noise each (2 s, filtered: a low-pass for rain, a band-pass for wind), not recordings, and play everywhere at once (no rain on a roof louder than in a field, no direction for the wind); thunder is one generated rumble per strike from the strike's loudness and length, not a recorded clap. | The mix curves are design choices, set at each update, smoothed by `@margoengine/audio` (LIM-394). | Rain and wind sound the same everywhere in the scene, and thunder is a generated rumble, not a recorded clap. | Pass your own `buffers` for recorded sound. |
| Real weather from METAR reports (`@margoengine/weather/data`, 2026-11-07) | By method: one report at a time, the observation only: the trend (NOSIG, BECMG, TEMPO) and remarks are kept as text, not decoded, and TAF forecasts are not read; runway visual range, runway state, wind shear and sea groups are skipped; cloud becomes the greatest layer's cover (no layer heights or types in the state), precipitation one of three intensities, and the state's fog comes from the prevailing visibility, so mist and haze read as fog by their visibility alone. | Astronomical sky (`@margoengine/sky/astro`, 2026-11-07) | No counted threshold; the planet elements are valid 1800 to 2050. | Each part uses a published method with a stated accuracy. | By method: the sun by Meeus' low-accuracy method (about 0.01 degree), the moon by his chapter 47 series (about 10 arcseconds) with its parallax, the planets by Standish's Keplerian elements (valid 1800 to 2050; tens of arcseconds, several arcminutes for Saturn), nutation by the short series (0.5 arcsecond); aberration (up to 20.5 arcseconds) is not applied, Saturn's magnitude leaves out its rings, and the planets are points, not discs. A fragment's `vertexIndex` and `instanceIndex` are the triangle's first vertex's. `modelMatrix` leaves out an instance's matrix. A depth pass reads the main camera's values (`positionView`, `linearDepth`, the matrices and camera planes), not the light's, and a `positionNode` that reads `tangentLocal`, `tangentWorld` or `bitangentWorld` casts the mesh unmoved. | A per-pixel frame from screen derivatives would line up with the UVs, but derivatives need uniform control flow and do not exist in a vertex stage; the fixed frame works in both stages and inside any branch. | `tangentWorld` on a mesh without tangents does not follow its UVs, and in a depth pass a `positionNode` that reads `tangentLocal`, `tangentWorld` or `bitangentWorld` casts the mesh unmoved; the camera values there are the main camera's, not the light's. | Workaround: `computeTangents` from `@margoengine/geometry`, or `varying()` for a per-vertex value. |
| Skinning and morph nodes (`@margoengine/shader/deform`, 2026-11-06) | By method: four bones per vertex, linear blending, so a bone with non-uniform scale skews `skin.normal()` and strong twists lose volume. `skinningFromModel(model, primitive)` reads a loaded glTF skin, refuses `JOINTS_1`, leaves morph targets to `morphing()`, keeps bind pose bounds, and `update()` reads the last transform update, so from `onFrame` the skin runs a frame behind the joints. | The graph runs where the pass runs, which is what lets an effect sit on top without a second vertex buffer. | Every pass that draws the mesh repeats the deformation: a pose costs 16 storage reads per vertex per pass, against one compute pass for `@margoengine/animation`. TAA velocity, CPU raycasts and BVH picking do not follow it, as for any `positionNode`: they see the bind pose. | Workaround: `@margoengine/animation` for a character with no effect in the vertex stage, or one reading `positionLocal` on top of its output. |
| Scene passes (`@margoengine/shader/pass`, 2026-11-06) | By method: opaque and masked gltf-pro surfaces only; blended surfaces, core meshes, the sky and other plugins are not in the pass, and `sceneColor` reads all of those but blended surfaces from the frame's own snapshot, for a surface that is `transparent: true`. Each model draws a second time, and `color` shades it twice. Targets are single-sampled, so edges in them are not antialiased. `velocity()` covers camera motion unless a mesh passes its previous position, and follows one camera: in a multi-view frame it holds the last view's matrix. Multi-view frames draw each view into its rectangle of the targets, but only a full-canvas view has a check, and `screenUV` is relative to the whole target. Formats must be filterable colour formats; `ScenePass` refuses `rgba32float` and integer formats. | The pass runs before the colour pass so a surface can read it in the same frame with no one-frame lag, which is what costs the second draw. `sceneColor` needs the opaque phase finished, so it costs a full-frame copy and sees no other blended surface. | Each model draws a second time and `color` shades it twice; edges in the targets are not antialiased. | Workaround: add the models that matter, and leave out what a surface need not see. |
| Utility nodes (`@margoengine/shader/utils`, 2026-11-06) | `normalMap` and `bumpNormal` work in fragment nodes only. | `parallaxUV` moves the texture lookup only, and blend modes follow the W3C formulas for colours from 0 to 1. | By method: `parallaxUV` moves the texture lookup only, so the outline stays flat and no shadow follows it; a `Texture` height is read at level 0, and views past about 84 degrees are held there. Blend modes are the W3C formulas for colours from 0 to 1, so HDR light above 1 clips. `triplanar` costs three reads per sample and blends colour only: it has no normal-map form. | Give `parallaxUV` a height function that samples with an explicit level (`texture(map, q, level).r`) in place of a `Texture` read at level 0; `PbrMaterial` with `triplanar: true` projects normal maps too. |
| Cellular noise on the GPU (`@margoengine/shader/noise`, 2026-11-06) | Distances are Euclidean only; there is no Manhattan or Chebyshev form. | By method: `voronoi2` and `voronoi3` search two cells each side, which is exact: 25 and 125 cells, three hashes each in 3D, so `voronoi3` and `worley3` cost far more per pixel than simplex. Not timed. | `voronoi3` and `worley3` cost far more per pixel than simplex. | Run it once in a compute pass, or at low resolution, and sample the result; on the CPU `new Noise(seed).worley(x, y, z)` gives the same field. |
